source: Landes E.; Francis K. B.; Everett J. A. C. — People defer to AI moral advice but not blindly
use: Direct evidence on persuasion and response-by-response deference to LLM moral advice
boundary: Three studies on everyday dilemmas; not evidence of universal behavior or moral superiority

source: Meincke L.; Nave G.; Terwiesch C. — Advice quality and source disclosure shape trust in AI-generated ethical advice
use: Compares GPT-4 ethical advice with New York Times Ethicist advice and studies source effects
boundary: Perceived usefulness and choice do not establish moral correctness or authority

source: Krügel S.; Ostermaier A.; Uhl M. — Justification optional: ChatGPT's advice can still influence human judgments about moral dilemmas
use: Evidence that chatbot advice can influence moral judgments even when justification effects are controlled
boundary: Vignette experiment; persuasion is not obedience and not legitimacy

source: Myers S.; Everett J. A. C. — People expect artificial moral advisors to be more utilitarian and distrust utilitarian moral advisors
use: Evidence on algorithm aversion and expectations that AI moral advisors will be utilitarian
boundary: Perceptions of advisors do not prove actual model behavior is inherently utilitarian

source: Leib M.; Köbis N.; Soraperra I. — Does AI and human advice mitigate punishment for selfish behavior?
use: Experimental evidence on harmful advice and responsibility judgments after AI or human advice
boundary: Specific incentivized design; not a general theory of responsibility

source: Giubilini A.; Savulescu J. — The Artificial Moral Advisor: The Ideal Observer Meets Artificial Intelligence
use: Strong affirmative case for an artificial moral advisor that helps users act on their own values
boundary: Proposal is philosophical and conditional rather than evidence that deployed systems currently satisfy the model

source: Rodríguez-López B.; Rueda J. — Artificial moral experts: asking for ethical advice to artificial intelligent assistants
use: Argument that some AI systems could qualify as artificial moral experts and provide useful advice
boundary: Moral expertise remains philosophically contested

source: Landes E.; Voinea C.; Uszkai R. — Rage against the authority machines: how to design artificial moral advisors for moral enhancement
use: Distinguishes moral enhancement from authority and argues for inspiration-oriented advisors
boundary: Normative proposal rather than settled empirical design law

source: Vallor S. — Moral Deskilling and Upskilling in a New Machine Age
use: Foundational account of technology-enabled moral deskilling and possible upskilling
boundary: Predates generative LLMs and should be applied by analogy with care

source: Hills A. — Moral Testimony
use: Overview of why moral testimony may differ from ordinary testimony and why understanding or character can matter
boundary: Does not establish that relying on moral testimony is always wrong

source: Epistemic Authorities and Skilled Agents: A Pluralist Account of Moral Expertise
use: Separates moral expertise as epistemic authority from expertise as skilled or virtuous agency
boundary: Supports plural conceptions rather than a single settled definition

source: Logg J. M.; Minson J. A.; Moore D. A. — Algorithm appreciation: People prefer algorithmic to human judgment
use: Shows that people can weight algorithmic advice more than human advice in some settings
boundary: Not specific to moral judgment and coexists with algorithm aversion literature

source: Goddard K.; Roudsari A.; Wyatt J. C. — Automation bias: Empirical results assessing influencing factors
use: Healthcare evidence that decision support can induce switching from correct to incorrect answers
boundary: Clinical decision support differs from generative moral advice

source: Human-AI Interactions in Public Sector Decision Making: Automation Bias and Selective Adherence to Algorithmic Advice
use: Counterevidence to a simplistic automation-bias story; finds no general automatic adherence in three public-sector experiments
boundary: Context specific and compares algorithmic predictions with human expert predictions

source: Engel C.; Hermstrüwer Y.; Kim A. — Human realignment: An empirical study of LLMs as legal decision-aids in moral dilemmas
use: Recent evidence of normative mismatches across models and mixed effects of explicit normative instruction
boundary: Classic dilemmas are proof-of-concept settings and not the whole of legal morality

source: Elish M. C. — Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction
use: Introduces moral crumple zone for misallocated human responsibility in complex automated systems
boundary: Concept should not be stretched to every human-in-the-loop arrangement

source: Delegated agency and moral responsibility in artificial intelligence
use: Recent conceptual distinctions among moral agency artificial agency delegated agency and moral authority
boundary: One normative account among contested positions on machine moral agency

source: Beckman L.; Hultin Rosenberg J.; Jebari K. — Artificial intelligence and democratic legitimacy: The problem of publicity in public authority
use: Separates accuracy and efficiency from democratic legitimacy and emphasizes accessible reasons
boundary: Focused on public authority rather than private moral advice

source: Are Algorithmic Decisions Legitimate? The Effect of Process and Outcomes on Perceptions of Legitimacy of AI Decisions
use: Experimental evidence on perceived legitimacy and appeal mechanisms
boundary: Perceived legitimacy is not identical to normative legitimacy

source: Gabriel I. — Artificial Intelligence Values and Alignment
use: Frames value alignment as a normative and political problem in a pluralistic world
boundary: Does not imply any one proposed alignment principle is settled

source: Schuster N.; Kilov D. — Moral disagreement and the limits of AI value alignment: a dual challenge of epistemic justification and political legitimacy
use: Direct analysis of reasonable moral disagreement and limits of crowdsourcing RLHF and constitutional approaches
boundary: Normative critique; future alignment methods may address some objections

source: Baum K.; Slavkovik M. — Aggregation Problems in Machine Ethics and AI Alignment
use: Distinguishes moral aggregation from social aggregation and shows that aggregation relocates normative commitments
boundary: Conceptual analysis rather than a claim that aggregation is useless

source: UNICEF — When AI becomes a friend: Child rights risks harms and regulatory responses to AI chatbots and companions
use: Child-rights analysis of chatbots and companions with policy recommendations
boundary: Risk-oriented policy evidence; not longitudinal proof of developmental harm

source: Hume D. — A Treatise of Human Nature Book III Part I Section I
use: Classic statement underlying the is/ought distinction
boundary: Interpretive use only; the manuscript does not claim facts are irrelevant to ethics

source: Plato — Euthyphro
use: Ancient dilemma about whether the good is good because authority approves it or authority approves it because it is good
boundary: Applied analogically to machine advice; not a historical claim about technology

source: Rawls J. — Political Liberalism
use: Reasonable pluralism public justification and political legitimacy
boundary: Book uses Rawls as one liberal framework not as a universal settlement of metaethics

source: Habermas J. — Between Facts and Norms
use: Public justification and legitimacy of binding authority
boundary: One theory of democratic legitimacy among alternatives

source: Estlund D. — Democratic Authority: A Philosophical Framework
use: Useful distinction between epistemic quality and legitimate political authority
boundary: Does not entail that expertise has no role in legitimate governance

source: Mill J. S. — On Liberty
use: Autonomy liberty experiments in living and limits based on harm
boundary: Nineteenth-century liberal framework requires modern qualification

source: Berlin I. — Two Concepts of Liberty
use: Pluralism and tensions between forms of liberty
boundary: Conceptual historical source not a direct AI governance prescription

source: Kant I. — Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
use: Counterweight to purely aggregative consequential reasoning through duties and persons
boundary: Used as philosophical contrast rather than a claim that one ethical theory wins

source: Bentham J. — An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
use: Historical consequentialist reference for utility and aggregation
boundary: Modern consequentialism is much broader than Bentham's formulation

source: UNESCO — Guidance for generative AI in education and research
use: Education governance developmental caution privacy and human-centered use
boundary: Policy guidance rather than causal developmental evidence

source: OECD — OECD AI Principles
use: Human-centered values accountability transparency robustness and governance context
boundary: High-level principles do not by themselves settle institutional design

source: NIST — Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework AI RMF 1.0
use: Governance accountability risk mapping measurement and management
boundary: Risk framework is not a theory of moral authority

source: Wallach W.; Allen C. — Moral Machines: Teaching Robots Right from Wrong
use: Foundational machine-ethics discussion of artificial moral agents and responsibility
boundary: Predates modern LLMs and should be used historically

source: Russell S. — Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control
use: Preference uncertainty and the problem of designing systems around human objectives
boundary: Technical alignment proposals do not settle pluralistic political legitimacy

source: Yeung L. K. C.; Tam C. S. Y.; Lau S. S. S.; Ko M. M. — Living with AI personal assistant: An ethical appraisal
use: Ethical analysis of AI personal assistants intimacy dependence privacy and autonomy
boundary: Personal assistants vary widely; risks are not inevitable outcomes

source: AI Deskilling and the Prospects for Public Reason
use: Connects AI deskilling with citizens' capacities for public reason
boundary: Normative argument rather than direct measurement of society-wide deskilling

source: Tocqueville A. de — Democracy in America Volume I Chapter XV
use: Historical observation connecting perceived collective intelligence with moral authority of the majority
boundary: Historical political analysis; not an argument that AI is a majority
